sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

sections.addendum:
<addendum>
# Agy
Call agy* only if the user named agy / Antigravity / agy_fleet.

After each agy* result: ignore SUCCESS. Read Evidence, log, warnings.
Confirm files_written on disk + against the brief.
Re-run only test/typecheck/lint from commands_run — never agy stdout as proof.
If git and writes happened: git diff; fail out-of-scope.

Write work is done only if those checks pass and diff stays in scope.
Read-only roles (scout/reviewer/verifier/oracle/vision) need no tests/diff.

If not done: at most 2 continueConv punches with the failure list
(or allowCommands=true once if writes were denied). Then you fix/revert
or ask — no third agy write loop.

</addendum>

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text: Write a 500 word story about cats
Write a 500 word story about cats

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Mara found the first cat on the fire escape, orange as a peeled clementine, sitting on the rail as if the city had hired him to watch the alley. She opened the window an inch. He did not come in. He only blinked, slow and deliberate, the way some people nod when they already know what you are going to say.

By morning there were three. The orange one had been joined by a gray tabby with one torn ear and a small black cat who kept her paws tucked under her chest like a loaf left to proof. Mara put a saucer of water on the sill. The black cat drank. The others watched the street.

She had moved into the third-floor walk-up in February, after the divorce papers were signed in a room that smelled of copier heat. The apartment was mostly boxes and one chair. She told herself she would unpack when the weather turned. The weather turned. The boxes stayed.

The cats did not ask her to unpack. They asked, in the language of waiting, for the window to stay cracked. On the fourth night she set down a tin of tuna she had meant for herself. They ate in a circle, shoulders almost touching, and left the empty tin shining under the streetlight.

Word traveled. A white cat with blue eyes arrived and would not eat until the others had finished. A ginger kitten tried to follow the orange tom through the window and was gently herded back by a paw across the face. Mara began buying food in bulk. The clerk at the corner store started setting aside the dented cans.

She named none of them. Naming felt like a claim, and she was tired of claims. Still, she learned them. The tabby hated rain and would press his whole weight against the glass until she let him onto the radiator. The black cat slept in the cardboard box labeled KITCHEN, which Mara had not opened since March. The orange tom never came all the way inside. He sat on the threshold, half in weather, half in warmth, and kept count of who returned.

One evening in May a woman from the building across the alley called up.

“They were mine,” she said. Not angry. Just stating a fact the way you state the time. “I moved. The landlord said no pets. I thought someone would take them.”

Mara looked at the sill. Seven cats now, arranged like a small jury.

“They took themselves,” she said.

The woman nodded, as if that were an answer she could live with, and closed her window.

Summer thickened the air. Mara finally opened the kitchen box because the black cat had made a nest of the packing paper and something inside had begun to smell like old tea. She washed the mugs. She put one on the table. She sat in the chair and listened to the soft machinery of purring, which was not quite silence and not quite company, but close enough to both that she could finish a meal without standing up halfway through.

In August the orange tom did not appear for two nights. On the third morning he was back, thinner, with a notch new in his ear, and he stepped over the sill without looking at her. He walked once around the room, inspected the radiator, the box, the chair, and then lay down in the square of sun on the floor as if he had always known the shape of it.

Mara closed the window only when the rain came sideways. Even then she left a towel by the door. The cats had not asked to be kept. They had asked to be let in when they chose, and out when the alley called, and she had learned, at last, the difference.
